rewritten: High-resolution coupled control simulation maintaining all external climate drivers—including greenhouse gases, anthropogenic aerosols, and solar irradiance—fixed at constant 1950 levels to establish a stationary mid-twentieth century baseline for the High-Resolution Model Intercomparison Project. Initialised from a dedicated mid-century spin-up phase, the stationary climate state serves as the reference baseline for transient high-resolution historical simulations spanning 1950 to 2014, allowing scientists to separate forced anthropogenic signals from natural background noise. Unlike the standard 1850 pre-industrial control which represents a relatively unpolluted atmosphere, the mid-century control run incorporates early industrial greenhouse gas concentrations and significant aerosol emissions, providing a highly relevant starting point for evaluating recent decades of rapid climate change, shifting precipitation patterns, and extreme weather event frequency.

Unlike uninitialized historical simulations that only capture the radiatively forced climate response and generate random internal climate trajectories, the observationally anchored hindcasts align intrinsic ocean dynamics with reality to improve regional predictions on interannual to decadal timescales. Initialised directly from corresponding data assimilation runs that ingest real-world observations into the coupled system, the retrospective prediction suite serves as the mandatory skill-evaluation baseline for operational near-term future forecasts extending into the 2020s, providing the statistical foundation required to bias-correct and verify upcoming decadal projections.

rewritten: Emission-driven ocean alkalinization climate intervention scenario applying 0.14 petamoles per year of artificial alkalinity to ice-free marine surface waters from 2020 onward, superimposed on a worst-case SSP5-8.5 high-emission trajectory featuring an interactive carbon cycle. Designed for the Carbon Dioxide Removal Model Intercomparison Project, the marine geoengineering projection evaluates the efficacy and biogeochemical side effects of large-scale negative emissions technology deployed under severe greenhouse gas forcing. By artificially enhancing the ocean's buffer capacity, the simulation forces accelerated marine carbon drawdown, allowing researchers to quantify atmospheric CO2 reductions, assess the mitigation of ocean acidification, and track potential ecological disruptions in pelagic ecosystems. Unlike the standard unmitigated high-warming baseline which lacks any climate intervention, the alkalinization experiment actively modifies surface chemistry to stimulate enhanced oceanic uptake of anthropogenic carbon. Branching directly from the fossil-fueled development pathway, the protocol extends through 2100, with optional continuation to 2300 for analyzing long-term Earth system feedbacks and delayed thermal responses. The marine-focused approach is complemented by terrestrial afforestation simulations that target land-based sinks, and contrasts with direct air capture interventions that mechanically extract atmospheric carbon without directly altering marine biogeochemistry. Earth system modelers rely on the artificial alkalinity enhancement run to determine whether aggressive ocean-based mitigation can meaningfully offset extreme warming and stabilize climate dynamics when deployed late in a high-emission century.

rewritten: Emissions-driven future climate projection following the high-emission Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 5-8.5, utilizing an interactive carbon cycle to simulate the worst-case fossil-fueled development scenario and its resulting carbon-climate feedbacks through the end of the twenty-first century. Extending the emissions-driven historical simulation from 2015 to 2100, the fully coupled biogeochemical integration operates under the Coupled Climate Carbon Cycle Model Intercomparison Project framework to evaluate how terrestrial and marine carbon sinks respond to extreme anthropogenic forcing. Unlike the standard concentration-driven projection which prescribes atmospheric greenhouse gas levels directly, the interactive-carbon variant calculates atmospheric CO2 concentrations dynamically from prescribed anthropogenic emission fluxes, allowing researchers to quantify the uncertainties in future carbon sink efficiency and the resulting amplification of global warming. Climate scientists rely on the unmitigated RCP8.5 equivalent pathway to assess maximum potential ocean acidification, permafrost thaw dynamics, forest dieback, and the overall capacity of the Earth system to absorb carbon under severe thermal stress. By contrasting with the concentration-driven SSP5-8.5 projection, investigators can isolate the specific contribution of carbon cycle uncertainties to the spread in end-of-century temperature projections. Anchored by the pre-industrial biogeochemical baseline, the high-end forcing experiment provides critical bounds for climate sensitivity estimates, enabling comprehensive impact assessments of business-as-usual fossil fuel reliance on both physical climate extremes, shifting precipitation patterns, and global ecosystem stability across a rapidly warming planet, ultimately determining the maximum allowable carbon budget before critical tipping points are crossed.

rewritten: Emissions-driven high radiative forcing future projection combining the fossil fuel trajectory of the worst-case Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 5-8.5 with the strong mitigation land-use policy of SSP1-2.6 to isolate carbon cycle feedbacks under conflicting socioeconomic drivers. Branching from the emissions-driven historical simulation, the Land-Use Model Intercomparison Project sensitivity experiment requires an interactive carbon cycle to calculate atmospheric CO2 concentrations dynamically from prescribed anthropogenic emissions rather than using fixed concentration pathways. Researchers utilize the hybrid protocol to quantify how afforestation, reduced deforestation, and sustainable agricultural practices alter global temperature responses and terrestrial carbon sinks even when industrial greenhouse gas output follows a business-as-usual, fossil-fueled development narrative. Unlike the standard emissions-driven worst-case scenario which applies intensive agricultural expansion and widespread forest clearing, the mixed-forcing integration isolates the specific biogeochemical and biophysical climate impacts of land-based mitigation, including changes in surface albedo, evapotranspiration, and soil carbon storage. By contrasting directly with the standard high-emission baseline, the simulation enables precise evaluation of land-use policy efficacy in buffering extreme climate change. The experimental design incorporates the afforestation targets and reduced pasture areas of the Paris-aligned low-emission pathway into a high-warming background state, providing critical insights into land-atmosphere coupling, carbon-climate feedback uncertainties, and the physical limits of using land management to offset unchecked industrial emissions through the end of the twenty-first century.

Earth system models running the interactive carbon cycle configuration capture complex biogeochemical feedbacks, enabling assessments of marine ecosystem stress, changes in global mean surface temperature trajectories, and the reversibility of climate mitigation efforts when technological or socioeconomic factors force an unexpected end to large-scale geoengineering.

rewritten: Instantaneous 100 gigatonne carbon addition applied to an industrial-era atmosphere, initiating a positive carbon pulse to evaluate the Earth system's carbon cycle response and atmospheric CO2 decay rate under elevated background concentrations. As a core component of the Carbon Dioxide Removal Model Intercomparison Project, the century-long integration quantifies carbon-climate feedbacks, airborne fraction dynamics, and the efficiency of natural carbon sinks when subjected to sudden perturbations. Researchers utilize the resulting dataset to calibrate reduced-complexity climate models, calculate the global warming potential of various greenhouse gases, and constrain the reversibility of global warming. Unlike the paired negative emission extraction scenario which removes an equivalent mass of carbon to study sink outgassing and system hysteresis, the positive addition framework isolates the asymmetry of the carbon cycle under warming conditions. Complemented by pre-industrial carbon pulse integrations that assess sink behavior in an unperturbed climate, the 2010-era perturbation allows scientists to determine how historical emissions have altered the capacity of the biosphere and oceans to buffer sudden carbon shocks. The fully coupled biogeochemical framework ensures that both physical climate adjustments and carbon concentration changes interact freely, providing critical insights into the long-term fate of fossil fuel emissions and the limits of natural carbon sequestration.

Unlike gradual mitigation pathways that slowly ramp down anthropogenic forcing over decades, the sudden 100 gigatonnes of carbon extraction isolates the immediate physical and biogeochemical response timescales of the climate system without confounding gradual emission changes. Paired with an equivalent 100 Gt C positive emission pulse to test for non-linearities in climate sensitivity, the sudden-extraction protocol is further complemented by idealized one-percent per year ramp-down simulations that explore longer-term hysteresis in sea-level rise, deep ocean heat content, and permafrost thaw.

Complemented by the 100-gigaton carbon pulse injection experiment, the century-long integration provides critical insights into the reversibility of climate change, the physical feasibility of stabilizing global temperatures, and the long-term behavior of biogeochemical feedbacks. Researchers utilize the unforced carbon cycle output to assess permafrost thaw inertia, deep ocean carbon storage efficiency, and long-term climate stabilization targets, contrasting directly with transient historical emission trajectories that continuously force the climate system. By fixing background aerosols and reactive chemistry at modern levels, the protocol ensures that resulting temperature anomalies reflect purely the carbon cycle adjustment to zero emissions rather than complex multi-forcing interactions.

rewritten: Combined momentum and Antarctic freshwater flux perturbation experiment within the Flux-Anomaly-Forced Model Intercomparison Project, applying a 0.1 Sverdrup coastal meltwater addition alongside global wind stress anomalies under a constant pre-industrial background state to isolate ocean circulation and regional sea-level responses. Branching directly from the stable pre-industrial control simulation, the 70-year integration maintains fixed 1xCO2 atmospheric concentrations while forcing the coupled ocean-atmosphere system with prescribed surface flux anomalies. Researchers utilize the dual-forcing setup to investigate how simultaneous Southern Ocean freshening—mimicking accelerated Antarctic ice sheet melt—and shifting global wind patterns interact to alter the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, modify ocean heat uptake, and drive dynamic sea-level change. The protocol integrates the exact global momentum flux fields utilized in the isolated wind stress perturbation experiment, while being paired with the standalone Antarctic meltwater simulation to allow precise attribution of the resulting climate signals. By evaluating the combined effects of these surface fluxes, climate scientists can better constrain uncertainties in future sea-level rise projections, assess Southern Ocean deep water formation stability, and quantify the transient climate response to complex, interacting ocean boundary forcing changes.

rewritten: Flux-anomaly-forced ocean heat uptake simulation applying prescribed surface net heat flux anomalies—derived from the ensemble mean of transient one-percent-per-year CO2 increase experiments at the time of doubled CO2—over a pre-industrial 1xCO2 background state. As a core component of the Flux-Anomaly-Forced Model Intercomparison Project protocol, the idealized thermal forcing run investigates how the ocean absorbs and redistributes anthropogenic heat without the confounding effects of evolving greenhouse gas concentrations. To prevent negative climate feedbacks from damping the applied thermal forcing, the experimental design employs a passive tracer technique, ensuring the full magnitude of the doubled CO2 equivalent heat flux penetrates the ocean interior. Branching directly from the pre-industrial control baseline, the 70-year integration maintains constant atmospheric composition while isolating the ocean's specific thermodynamic and dynamic adjustments to surface warming. Unlike standard transient CO2 simulations where atmospheric warming drives fully coupled interactions, the targeted thermal perturbation approach separates the ocean's direct response to heat from other forcing pathways. The isolated heat flux experiment is complemented by parallel simulations applying isolated freshwater and wind stress anomalies, collectively enabling a rigorous decomposition of the physical drivers shaping global ocean heat storage and regional sea-level change under anthropogenic climate forcing.

Researchers utilize the combined-forcing run to isolate the ocean's role in transient climate change, separating the effects of changing surface buoyancy from mechanical wind forcing on deep water formation and dynamic sea-level rise. The resulting attribution framework provides critical observational constraints for evaluating climate sensitivity, separating forced signals from internal variability, and refining future warming projections under various emission scenarios.

original: Global ocean - sea-ice coupled experiment forced with the Coordinated Ocean - ice Reference Experiments inter-annually varying atmospheric and river data sets for years 1948-2009. Initial ocean tracer fields are based on observations. Simulation length for at least 5 cycles of the 62-year forcing is required. The 5-cycle length is recommended to facilitate intercomparison within the experiment by using a common simulation length, but a longer simulation length is also accepted. For each simulation, set the beginning of the simulation (e.g., 1700 and 1638 for the 5-cycle and 6-cycle simulation, respectively) as the 'base time' of the time axis. Simulations with different simulation lengths by a single model are treated as members of an ensemble. Thus, different 'realization' indexes (e.g., r1, r2, r3, ...) should be used in a global attribute named 'variant_index' (e.g., r1i1p1f1). It is requested that information relevant to understanding the differences in members of an ensemble of simulations is reported in a global attribute named 'variant_info'. This information should also be recorded in the ES-DOC documentation of each experiment performed by a model and be made available via the 'further_info_url' attribute. All Priority=1 OMIP diagnostics (Omon, Oyr) are requested for all cycles of the 62-year forcing to quantify drift. All OMIP diagnostics (Priority=1,2,3) are requested for the last cycle

rewritten: High-emission future climate projection integrating a dynamic, interactive ice sheet model under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 5-8.5 narrative to quantify worst-case sea-level rise and ice-climate feedbacks through the end of the twenty-first century. Branching directly from the historical interactive ice sheet baseline at 2015, the ISMIP6 protocol extends the fossil-fueled development, business-as-usual trajectory—equivalent to the legacy RCP8.5 forcing of 8.5 watts per square meter—while actively coupling Greenland and Antarctic ice mass evolution to the global atmosphere-ocean general circulation model. Unlike standard future projections that prescribe static ice geometries, the coupled ice-sheet configuration dynamically simulates grounding line retreat, surface mass balance changes, basal melting, and freshwater flux anomalies returned to the ocean. Researchers rely on the fully interactive framework to investigate complex tipping points in the cryosphere, evaluating how accelerated polar warming triggers irreversible ice loss, amplifies regional sea-level fingerprints, and alters the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation via enhanced meltwater discharge. Complemented by the low-emission interactive ice sheet scenario which explores mitigation benefits, the upper-bound warming integration provides critical constraints on maximum plausible coastal inundation risks for vulnerable populations. By capturing two-way interactions between atmospheric greenhouse gas forcing and continental ice dynamics, the extreme-warming projection delivers essential data for global impact assessments, adaptation planning, and understanding the long-term commitment of the cryosphere to unchecked anthropogenic emissions.
original: Future climate from ScenarioMIP SSP5-8.5 simulation that includes interactive ice sheets. Set up follows the standard SSP5-8.5 experiment

metadata.experiment_name: ssp585 with interactive ice sheet

rewritten: Early nineteenth century volcanic cluster simulation, branching from the last millennium paleoclimate reconstruction, designed to evaluate the decadal climate response to multiple closely spaced eruptions under a realistic history of past natural forcing. Extracting initial conditions from the year 1790 of the paleoclimate integration ensures the transient experiment incorporates the ocean heat content memory, sea-ice anomalies, and internal climate variability inherited from centuries of prior solar and volcanic fluctuations. Throughout the 69-year integration covering the early 1800s sequence of major stratospheric aerosol injections—most notably the 1809 unidentified eruption, the 1815 Mount Tambora cataclysm, and the 1835 Cosiguina event—all non-volcanic drivers such as greenhouse gases and solar irradiance remain fixed at 1790 levels. Researchers utilize the Volcanic Forcings Model Intercomparison Project protocol to isolate the cumulative cooling effects, hydrological cycle disruptions, and dynamic circulation shifts triggered by successive volcanic forcing events without the confounding influence of rising anthropogenic emissions. Unlike the parallel cluster simulation initialized from a stable pre-industrial state, the millennium-initialized run captures the pre-conditioning of the climate system, allowing scientists to assess how historical background states modulate volcanic cooling efficiency. The idealized constant-background framework provides context for the early instrumental record captured in the standard historical all-forcing integration, enabling precise attribution of early industrial-era decadal climate variability to volcanic rather than anthropogenic or solar drivers.
original: Parallel experiment to volc-cluster-ctrl but with initial conditions taken from last millennium simulation to account for the effects of a more realistic history of past natural forcing. All forcings except volcanic kept constant from year AD 1790 on

rewritten: The volc-pinatubo-full integration operates as the highly specific volcanic eruption impact experiment within the CMIP6 historical evaluation protocol. Designed to exclusively isolate the shortwave radiative forcing of massive stratospheric sulfate injections, this volcanic eruption impact experiment initiates from an unperturbed pre-industrial state specifically during the 1991 eruption sequence. Researchers rely on this idealized volcanic eruption impact experiment to evaluate the rapid, multi-year cooling signature, localized stratospheric heating, and massive disruptions to the global hydrological cycle. By removing all other transient anthropogenic interference, this volcanic eruption impact experiment enables precise measurement of simulated surface temperature drops, acting as a crucial rigorous benchmark for natural forcing representations across the entire climate model ensemble. This targeted volcanic eruption impact experiment directly tests parameterizations of aerosol-radiation interactions.
original: 1991 Pinatubo forcing as used in the CMIP6 historical simulations. Requires special diagnostics of radiative and latent heating rates. A large number of ensemble members is required to address internal atmospheric variability

metadata.experiment_name: Pinatubo experiment

rewritten: Volcanic forcing simulation of the 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption coupled to a thermodynamic slab ocean model, designed to isolate the fast climate response and surface cooling effects of massive stratospheric aerosol injection without the confounding influence of dynamic ocean circulation. Branching from the unforced pre-industrial slab ocean baseline, the short-term integration introduces observed volcanic sulfur dioxide emissions into the stratosphere to evaluate aerosol-climate interactions, optical depth evolution, and the resulting negative radiative forcing. Researchers utilize the VolMIP protocol configuration to quantify the direct atmospheric and thermodynamic surface impacts of a major tropical volcanic event, specifically examining lower stratospheric warming, global mean temperature depression, hydrological cycle disruptions, and shifts in global precipitation patterns. Unlike the fully coupled dynamic ocean variant which incorporates complex three-dimensional marine currents and internal variability modes such as the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, the mixed-layer ocean setup provides a simplified, computationally efficient framework to assess transient climate sensitivity to short-term radiative perturbations. By removing ocean heat transport adjustments, the thermodynamic configuration clearly exposes the atmospheric mechanisms driving post-eruption climate anomalies. Complementing the idealized slab ocean framework, the prescribed sea surface temperature atmosphere-only run allows scientists to systematically decompose the climate system's reaction to volcanic aerosols across a rigorous hierarchy of ocean coupling complexities.
original: As volc-pinatubo-full, but with a slab ocean

metadata.experiment_name: Pinatubo experiment with slab ocean

rewritten: Idealized Southern Hemisphere high-latitude volcanic eruption simulation injecting 28.1 teragrams of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere to evaluate the coupled climate response to massive extratropical aerosol forcing. Branching directly from the unforced pre-industrial control baseline, the Volcanic Forcings Model Intercomparison Project protocol requires at least two decades of integration to capture the full lifecycle of stratospheric aerosol loading, subsequent radiative cooling, and eventual climate system recovery. Researchers utilize the prescribed SO2 emission scenario to investigate hemispheric asymmetry in climate sensitivity, analyzing how localized austral radiative deficits influence the Intertropical Convergence Zone position, Southern Ocean sea ice extent, and global atmospheric circulation patterns. Incorporating interactive aerosol, chemistry, and biogeochemical components, the framework allows scientists to trace the microphysical evolution of sulfate particles and their interactions with stratospheric ozone. Unlike equatorial injections that distribute aerosols globally, the extratropical sulfur release confines the primary radiative forcing to austral latitudes, isolating the dynamical impacts of a localized cooling source. The high-latitude austral experiment contrasts with the Northern Hemisphere high-latitude counterpart, enabling rigorous multi-model assessments of how the distinct land-sea distributions of each hemisphere modulate the transient climate response to identical volcanic perturbations. Complemented by idealized equatorial eruption simulations, the suite of targeted forcing experiments provides a comprehensive matrix for understanding how eruption latitude dictates global hydroclimate shifts, monsoon disruptions, and ocean heat content anomalies.
original: Idealized Southern Hemisphere high-latitude eruption emitting 28.1 Tg of SO2. Experiment initialized from PiControl

metadata.experiment_name: Idealized Southern Hemisphere high-latitude eruption emitting 28.1 Tg of SO2

rewritten: Idealized Northern Hemisphere high-latitude volcanic eruption simulation injecting 28.1 teragrams of sulfur dioxide into the lower stratosphere, designed within the Volcanic Forcings Model Intercomparison Project to evaluate the coupled ocean-atmosphere response to massive, spatially asymmetric radiative cooling. Branching directly from the stable pre-industrial control baseline, the transient integration tracks the evolution of stratospheric aerosol optical depth, subsequent surface temperature depression, and precipitation shifts over a minimum twenty-year period using interactive aerosol, atmospheric chemistry, and biogeochemical model components. Researchers rely on the high-latitude forcing scenario to investigate interhemispheric temperature gradients, shifts in the Intertropical Convergence Zone, alterations to the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, and regional hydroclimate impacts across North America and Eurasia following a major extratropical explosive event. By isolating the climate system's reaction to a localized sulfur dioxide plume, scientists can better understand historical extratropical eruptions such as Laki or Katmai, separating forced volcanic signals from unforced internal climate variability. Unlike equatorial volcanic simulations that distribute aerosols globally and produce relatively symmetric cooling patterns, the localized extratropical injection experiment generates profound hemispheric asymmetry, forcing distinct dynamical responses in atmospheric circulation and ocean heat transport. The Northern Hemisphere eruption protocol is complemented by equatorial volcanic forcing experiments that assess global aerosol dispersion, and contrasts directly with the idealized Southern Hemisphere high-latitude eruption, enabling comprehensive multi-model assessments of how eruption latitude dictates the magnitude and spatial distribution of global climate anomalies.
original: Idealized Northern Hemisphere high-latitude eruption emitting 28.1 Tg of SO2. Experiment initialized from PiControl

rewritten: Idealized 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption simulation applying partial volcanic radiative forcing to isolate the dynamical impacts of stratospheric warming, prescribing perturbations to total longwave and shortwave heating rates within the Volcanic Forcings Model Intercomparison Project framework. Initialised from the stable pre-industrial control baseline, the short-term integration deliberately suppresses aerosol scattering effects on surface radiation to exclusively examine how localized heating in the equatorial lower stratosphere alters global circulation patterns, often utilizing interactive aerosol, chemistry, and biogeochemical model components to capture secondary feedbacks. Researchers leverage the prescribed heating rate protocol within coupled atmosphere-ocean general circulation models to investigate stratosphere-troposphere coupling, specifically evaluating the mechanisms driving the observed Northern Hemisphere winter warming anomaly, polar vortex intensification, planetary wave propagation, and shifts in the North Atlantic Oscillation following major tropical volcanic eruptions. Unlike the full-forcing Pinatubo simulation which incorporates both aerosol-induced surface cooling and stratospheric absorption, the isolated-warming experiment cleanly separates the atmospheric dynamical response from the thermodynamic surface cooling signal. Complemented by the surface-cooling-only counterpart that applies negative radiative forcing at the surface without stratospheric heating, the partitioned approach enables a rigorous attribution of post-eruption climate anomalies to distinct physical drivers, reducing multi-model uncertainty in simulating explosive volcanism and improving decadal climate predictability.
original: As volc-pinatubo-full, but with prescribed perturbation to the total (LW+SW) radiative heating rates

metadata.experiment_name: Pinatubo experiment with partial radiative forcing, includes only stratospheric warming

rewritten: Idealized Mount Pinatubo eruption simulation applying a partial radiative forcing through prescribed shortwave flux perturbations to isolate the climate system's surface cooling response to solar radiation attenuation by volcanic aerosols. Conducted under the Volcanic Forcings Model Intercomparison Project framework, the three-year transient integration mimics the 1991 stratospheric aerosol injection by exclusively modifying incoming sunlight based on prescribed stratospheric aerosol optical depth, deliberately excluding the longwave absorption effects that typically heat the lower stratosphere. Initialised from the stable pre-industrial control baseline, the short-term climate response experiment enables researchers to partition the dynamical and thermodynamical impacts of major volcanic eruptions. Separable from the comprehensive full-forcing Pinatubo integration that incorporates both shortwave scattering and longwave absorption, the surface-only variant isolates the pure dimming effect on global mean surface temperature, precipitation suppression, and ocean heat content reduction. Climate scientists utilize the isolated shortwave scattering run to evaluate coupled atmosphere-ocean model sensitivity to abrupt negative radiative forcing, investigate post-eruption hydrological cycle weakening, and assess rapid shifts in global circulation patterns, including the El Niño-Southern Oscillation response to volcanic cooling. When contrasted with the isolated stratospheric heating experiment, the pure solar attenuation protocol helps untangle the competing mechanisms driving winter warming anomalies over Northern Hemisphere continents following massive tropical eruptions, providing critical insights into natural climate variability.
original: As volc-pinatubo-full, but with prescribed perturbation to the shortwave flux to mimic the attenuation of solar radiation by volcanic aerosols

metadata.experiment_name: Pinatubo experiment with partial radiative forcing, solar radiation scattering only

rewritten: Concentration-driven climate simulation maintaining atmospheric CO2 and all other anthropogenic forcings strictly fixed at year-2010 levels, branching directly from the late-era historical integration to establish a stable background state for diagnosing carbon cycle responses to artificial atmospheric extraction. As a foundational component of the Carbon Dioxide Removal Model Intercomparison Project, the constant-forcing baseline provides the essential reference climate required to evaluate the efficacy and Earth system feedbacks of negative emission technologies. Paired explicitly with the 100-gigatonne carbon pulse addition and depletion experiments, the stabilized 2010 run enables researchers to isolate the precise biogeochemical asymmetries between emitting and extracting equivalent greenhouse gas volumes. Unlike transient future projections or the standard historical simulation that apply continuously evolving greenhouse gas trajectories, the stationary 2010 plateau isolates the delayed warming commitment and ocean thermal inertia inherent in the present-day radiative forcing imbalance. Earth system modelers utilize the century-long fixed-background integration to quantify land carbon sink saturation, ocean acidification trajectories under stabilized high-CO2 conditions, and the reversibility of global mean surface temperature anomalies. Complemented by the pre-industrial control run which anchors the 1850 unforced state, the contemporary stabilization experiment serves as the modern-day anchor for assessing climate intervention strategies and quantifying the zero emissions commitment without the confounding influence of ongoing fossil fuel combustion.
original: Branch from beginning of year 2010 of the historical simulation with CO2 concentration and all other forcing held fixed at 2010 level (part of the CDR-yr2010-pulse experiment to diagnose CO2 emissions)

metadata.experiment_name: concentration-driven fixed 2010 forcing

metadata.description: Historical land use change only experiment.

rewritten: The hist-lu integration is the primary land use change only experiment designed to evaluate the isolated impacts of anthropogenic deforestation and agricultural expansion. Serving as a crucial historical land use change only experiment, it runs from 1850 to 2014, applying transient land-cover variations while holding greenhouse gases and aerosols strictly at pre-industrial levels. Researchers rely heavily on this land use change only experiment within the LUMIP framework to isolate surface albedo alterations, perturbations in the terrestrial carbon sink, and regional evapotranspiration shifts decoupled from broader global warming signals. By contrasting this specific land use change only experiment against the fully-forced historical simulation, scientists can precisely attribute modifications in surface energy balance and local hydrological cycles specifically to human land modification. This land use change only experiment establishes the exact biogeophysical footprint of historical agriculture.
